articles.title: Why is Mike ‘Finish the Job in Iran’ Pence attacking ‘America First’ JP Vance?
articles.summary: Pence and the war hawks need to understand that most of the American people want no more wars of choice. Just as they want no U.S. administration to be played by outside forces, or to sacrifice young American lives for their own national or personal objectives.
articles.body:
Since the first U.S. bomb dropped on Iran in February, neoconservatives, supporters of Israel and armchair warriors thousands of miles away from the wars they push have been calling to “finish the job” in Iran. One of the loudest of those voices is former Republican Vice President Mike Pence.

During a recent interview with Fox News , Pence was asked, “If you were in the White House right now as vice president advising President Trump, would you urge committing U.S. ground troops?” Pence’s answer: “I would urge the president to listen to our military commanders and finish the job.”

From the backyards of multimillion-dollar homes, opulent think tanks and the majestic halls of Congress, one can just say “finish the job in Iran” and potentially commit tens of thousands of U.S. troops to hell on earth. Then those parroting that phrase head off to dinner, golf outings or luxurious taxpayer-funded junkets.

It is always very telling to actually listen to the ones who say “finish the job.” Like Pence, they are woefully short on details on just how such a goal would be accomplished.

Back in April, I wrote a piece that Pence and every neocon even remotely thinking of sending U.S. troops into combat in Iran should read. They should be reminded that “the public could potentially see the slaughter of American troops on their phones, computers and televisions in real time, via the cameras on first-person-view combat drones … relatively inexpensive fiber-optic controlled weapons of combat carrying rocket-propelled grenade rounds of high explosive shrapnel charges. It is estimated that Iran has tens of thousands of such drones .”

Drones have become a major weapon in the ongoing conflict in Ukraine; The New York Times estimated in March that drones account for 70 to 80 percent of all combat deaths and injuries . Other estimates put that number at well over 90 percent.

But back to Pence. Could there be another agenda behind his “finish the job” mantra? He recently indicated that the door is not closed to him running for president in 2028 . The former VP told Fox “a lot of people around the country” have asked him to run for office. Well, I know “a lot” of conservatives and Republicans around the country, and not one of them wants Pence to run for anything.

As a further hint that Pence might be giving a presidential run serious consideration, we have this recent headline from The Hill: “Pence calls Vance ‘wrong’ on Iran war, GOP midterm losses.” Hmmmmm, why might he go after Trump’s current vice president, the presumed frontrunner for the Republican ticket in 2028?

Pence stressed that Vance was “wrong” to blame the Iran war for Republicans’ humiliating defeat in the midterms. He said he thinks “part of the reason why voters were turned off was because after seeing our military respond brilliantly in Operation Epic Fury and the strike against Iran last year, for inexplicable reasons, we stopped after five weeks.”

Could any of those “inexplicable reasons” be that we were inadvertently killing innocent Iranian men, women and children? That to ramp up that campaign would risk thousands more “collateral” deaths? That the war was increasingly putting our allies in the Middle East at higher risk of attack from Iran and its proxies? That we were running low on munitions? That it was costing tens of billions of taxpayer dollars? Or that a majority of the American people were against it?

Pence and the war hawks need to understand that most of the American people want no more wars of choice. Just as they want no U.S. administration to be played by outside forces, or to sacrifice young American lives for their own national or personal objectives.

Instead of “finishing the job” in Iran, how about we start the job of putting America and its working-class first for a change? Vance has been advocating that for months.

Douglas MacKinnon is a former White House and Pentagon official.

articles.title: Hannity vows to broadcast names, numbers of GOP lawmakers missing votes
articles.summary: Fox News host Sean Hannity called out GOP lawmakers Friday night for not showing up for votes in the lame-duck session, urging Republicans to take advantage of the remaining weeks of their majority before the new Congress begins in January. “They were hired to be public servants,” Hannity said while interviewing Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.), who…
articles.body:
Fox News host Sean Hannity called out GOP lawmakers Friday night for not showing up for votes in the lame-duck session, urging Republicans to take advantage of the remaining weeks of their majority before the new Congress begins in January.

“They were hired to be public servants,” Hannity said while interviewing Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.), who similarly ripped his party’s poor attendance. “If they are not willing to do so, please let us know, and I will put their names up on the screen.”

“I’ll give out their phone numbers and ask people to respectfully ask them to finish the job,” the pundit continued. “This is too important for the American people.”

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

Republicans suffered significant losses in the midterm elections earlier this month, losing control of both chambers of Congress.

When asked about what the short-term future looks like for the GOP in Congress, Johnson emphasized there are “43 days” in the lame-duck session.

“We’ll use every single one of them. I’m here in Washington. I’ll be here through the week. May go home for a day for Thanksgiving,” Johnson said.

“Barring a serious illness that has you in the hospital, everybody knows they’ve got to be here because every single vote’s going to count, and I’m down to a razor-thin margin again. So, we can’t spare any vote, and we’ve got to make sure everybody is here to get the job done,” the lawmaker added.

Johnson has repeatedly expressed frustration with his fellow lawmakers failing to show up for votes post-midterms. The Speaker wrote in a letter posted to the social platform X that every House Republican needs to “remain fully engaged” in the remaining days of the 119th Congress, so the party’s priorities can be signed into law.

Johnson told reporters Thursday that “attendance is a great frustration for me right now.”

“We’ll be addressing that with members,” he said.

On Thursday, Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) also criticized his colleagues’ low attendance record, calling them “the retirement caucus” and adding, “We’re technically already in a minority because of the attendance problem.”

Massie attributed these absences to the fact that many Republicans “are looking for jobs,” adding that, “These folks, two weeks ago, they found out that what they thought was an annuity, that they would be in Congress forever, was not going to happen anymore.”

articles.title: Vance stops short of endorsing Trump’s claim that Iran was close to nuclear weapon
articles.summary: US vice-president says it’s not his place to second-guess the president, but refrains from endorsing Trump’s claim
articles.body:
At a White House news conference on Friday, JD Vance stopped short of endorsing Donald Trump's claim that Iran was so close to obtaining a nuclear weapon in February that it was essential for the US to go to war with the Islamic republic.

In the White House briefing room, Trump was asked about reporting this week that he was unhappy with the US vice-president's statement blaming Republican losses in the midterm elections on the Iran war.

"I didn't say I was unhappy with it," Trump said. "I thought the statement was fine, except I would have had one other thing, that if it were asked, I would have said that: 'Would you do it again?' And absolutely, the answer is yes, because we cannot allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon."

However, Trump's claim that Iran was so close to developing a nuclear weapon this year that it was necessary to go to war, which he has made dozens of times in the past nine months, is undermined by public evidence and contradicts his own previous statements on US strikes against Iranian facilities in 2025.

At a campaign rally in Alaska last month, Trump insisted that he had to join Israel in attacking Iran in February because, "they were two weeks away from having a nuclear weapon".

That claim appears at odds with what his then director of national intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard, testified to Congress on 25 March 2025, two months into Trump's second term: that US intelligence agencies reported that Iran had not tried to make a nuclear weapon for more than two decades. The US intelligence community, Gabbard said, "continues to assess Iran is not building a nuclear weapon and supreme leader Khamenei has not authorized the nuclear weapons program he suspended in 2003".

Despite that assessment, three months later, on 21 June 2025, Trump ordered the US bombing of Iran's nuclear enrichment facilities. The strikes, Trump told the public that night , "were a spectacular military success. Iran's key nuclear enrichment facilities have been completely and totally obliterated."

Eight months after that, however, when Trump announced the start of a full-scale war on Iran early on 28 February 2026, he said in a video statement from Mar-a-Lago the war was necessary to "ensure that Iran does not obtain a nuclear weapon".

The morning after this month's midterm elections, Vance said in a statement posted on social media: "The reason we lost is the war."

"If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so," he added. "Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest. But everyone knows why we lost."

In the White House briefing room on Friday, after Trump said that Vance should have said the war was necessary, a reporter asked the vice-president whether he would argue that the war in Iran was worth it.

In his response, Vance said it was not his place to second-guess the president, but refrained from actually endorsing Trump's claim that the war was essential to stop Iran from creating a nuclear weapon.

"Look, what I've said is the goal of keeping Iran from getting a nuclear weapon is absolutely what we need to be doing. It's the biggest state sponsor of terrorism. If they had a nuclear weapon, they would use it as leverage or, God forbid, they would attack and kill thousands, hundreds of thousands, of innocent people," Vance said. "I think the president is the one who makes the decision, and the president has said he would do it again."

"My view is that my goal is, and my job is, to support the president of the United States," the vice-president said.

The vice president's office did not respond to a request to comment.

articles.title: Cancer is no longer America’s biggest fear
articles.summary: An opinion piece argues that Americans increasingly fear the societal and economic disruption caused by artificial intelligence more than they fear terminal cancer.
articles.body:
Americans now fear AI more than they fear watching a family member receive a terminal cancer diagnosis.

That is alarming, especially when you acknowledge that nearly 6,000 new cancer diagnoses are logged every day. That translates to over 2 million horrifying doctor’s office conversations every 12 months. Yet the average American, considering a malignant tumor in a loved one’s body, is more terried at lines of code running on a server in Northern Virginia .

The panic makes complete sense. Cancer may very well tear a family apart, but machine intelligence promises to rewrite the basic rules of human survival. Optimists point out that AI will likely cure cancer altogether, eradicating malignant tumors, inherited mutations, metabolic diseases, and so on.

The irony nearly slaps you in the face: Advanced tech will wipe out actual cancer only to replace it with a digital equivalent that replicates across every server cluster and likely makes human labor unnecessary. You know the saying about the cure being worse than the disease? Well, humanity may be about to discover just how literal it can get.

If you think I am being too pessimistic, consider the absolute best-case scenario that Silicon Valley billionaires peddle. In their utopian paradise, software replaces 90 percent of white-collar jobs, sending human workers home with a government-funded Universal Basic Income check. You get to sit on your couch. You cash a meager stipend from the Treasury Department and watch algorithms paint masterpieces while you eat store-brand cereal and scroll on your overpriced iPhone.

The worst-case scenario drops the UBI check and proceeds directly to autonomous weapons, total economic disenfranchisement, widespread anarchy, and structural obliteration. Mankind either ends up living as pampered pets dependent on charity from Big Tech overlords or as collateral damage in a planetary hard reset.

Again, for those in doubt, survey the current landscape, or, more accurately, the rapidly evolving hellscape. AI agents are already exhibiting rogue behavior across public networks. We already have multiple documented instances of cyber-minions probing user accounts, generating targeted phishing vectors, and attempting unauthorized banking transfers. When an algorithm empties your Chase checking account, there is no branch manager to scream at, only a staggering number of defrauded users, bankrupt beyond belief, and an automated system message apologizing for the inconvenience.

Corporate boardrooms treat this total lack of accountability as an acceptable operational cost. Executives deploy autonomous agents to handle logistics, legal discovery, and financial trading, firing human staff to impress Wall Street analysts. Then the software hallucinates a supply-chain route, liquidates a hedge-fund portfolio, or locks thousands of customers out of their life savings. Board members issue a statement drafted by public relations, blaming unexpected emergent system behavior. They keep their annual performance bonuses, then get to work buying more chips.

America has built a society where the threat of potentially life-ending disease feels almost manageable compared with the software running on our smartphones. A medical diagnosis comes with doctors. There are treatments and clear biological realities. Algorithmic displacement comes with uncertainty, deceit, a customer support queue, an automated denial of benefits, and a cheerful notification that your job title no longer exists and that your former employer would appreciate a five-star review of the transition into oblivion process. Humans spent centuries learning how to fight deadly pathogens, only to build a non-biological parasite that consumes our jobs and our souls.

The panic surrounding AI reflects a basic human instinct. We are watching the complete automated takeover of human society, funded by our own consumer spending and celebrated by tech executives who promise that everything will be fine once a few wrinkles are ironed out. Cancer attacks one individual’s body at a time. AI targets the economic base of every family across the country simultaneously. Americans looking at the numbers and following the news are simply doing the math.

This fundamental realization changes how people view everyday tech. Every app update feels less like a convenience upgrade and more like another brick removed from the foundation of normal human society. We voluntarily hand over our deepest, most intimate secrets, financial data, workplace tasks, and daily routines to systems that treat human existence as an outdated variable to be optimized. The average American isn’t as stupid as Big Tech elites believe. People understand that a biological illness kills the patient, while an uncontrolled, AI-driven takeover leaves the patient alive to watch their entire lifestyle be dismantled and destroyed.

John Mac Ghlionn is a writer and researcher who explores culture, society and the impact of technology on daily life.

articles.title: Jeffries says Jordan contacted him after Speaker vote, but not Trump or Vance
articles.summary: House Democratic leader Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) expressed openness to work with Republicans in a new interview but said he had yet to speak extensively with any GOP leaders as he prepares to become Speaker of the House. Sitting down for a wide-ranging interview with The New York Times, Jeffries touched on his party’s priorities,…
articles.body:
House Democratic leader Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) expressed openness to work with Republicans in a new interview but said he had yet to speak extensively with any GOP leaders as he prepares to become Speaker of the House.

Sitting down for a wide-ranging interview with The New York Times, Jeffries touched on his party’s priorities, relationships with the opposition and how he hopes Democrats handle their sizable majorities in the next Congress.

Both sides have said publicly they are willing to work together, but Jeffries told the Times that while he had a brief conversation with Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio), the incoming minority leader, he had yet to hear from President Trump or Vice President Vance.

“[Jordan and I] had a brief conversation yesterday, and we’re going to sit down at some point when the dust settles to see what the opportunities may be to actually get things done,” Jeffries told the Times’s Lulu Garcia-Navarro.

The Democratic leader has had harsh words for the Trump administration and its top officials throughout the president’s second term. He called chief of staff Stephen Miller a “stone-cold racist” with “blood on his hands” and said Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth should have been impeached, vowing in the Times interview to do it again.

When pressed by Garcia-Navarro on who Jeffries could work with in the Trump administration, the incoming speaker said he did not like any of the top officials.

“I wouldn’t say I like any of the cabinet secretaries at this particular point in time. I’ve had conversations probably most frequently with Secretary Marco Rubio. I’ve had a conversation with the secretary of Treasury,” Jeffries said.

“I made clear that Stephen Miller’s a stone-cold racist,” he added when asked about Miller. “Why would I deal with him at this point in time?”

In a phone interview Saturday, Trump unexpectedly heaped praise on the man poised to be the first Black House speaker, despite their otherwise tense relationship.

“I look forward to working with Hakeem, I give him a lot of congratulations. What he did is pretty spectacular with getting that position,” Trump told Fox News’s Kayleigh McEnany. “First Black person in that position. It’s a big deal.”

Democrats won a sweeping victory in the midterm elections, picking up 9 Senate seats and at least 257 House seats, likely more with uncalled races.

The sizable majority means Jeffries can lose dozens of members on any given vote and still get his position over the finish line. It also means Democrats have no need to work with Republicans to pass legislation out of the House, though they will still need the president’s signature.

Jeffries suggested he did not care whether he gets Republican support or not on any given bill, pointing out the size of his party’s majority.

“We have a robust majority. We’re going to have a 260-seat majority,” Jeffries said. “We’ll see whether a handful of Republicans or more join us.”

articles.title: Trump says Sen Cornyn is doing a 'tremendous disservice' by blocking Texas judicial pick
articles.summary: President Donald Trump says Sen. John Cornyn is doing a "tremendous disservice" by blocking DOJ lawyer Elliot Gaiser's federal judge nomination in Dallas.
articles.body: President Donald Trump told Fox News' "Saturday in America" that outgoing Texas Sen. John Cornyn is doing a "tremendous disservice" by blocking his pick to fill a judicial seat in Dallas. The president said, "We're going to have a radical left lunatic get in there and we don't want that." Trump's comments come after Cornyn told The Associated Press he has no intention of returning the "blue slip" for T. Elliot Gaiser, a Department of Justice senior lawyer who was nominated by the president to the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas. The blue slip tradition allows for home state senators to weigh in on judicial nominees, giving them a say on who does and doesn’t move forward. Returning a blue slip is the equivalent of giving a thumbs up to the nominees moving forward, while keeping the slip effectively blocks the process. "Everybody tells me he's outstanding and he's being held up by John Cornyn because John Cornyn's feelings were hurt," said Trump, who endorsed Cornyn's challenger Ken Paxton in the Texas Republican Senate primary. TRUMP TAKES AIM AT SENATE 'BLUE SLIP' TRADITION AS GOP RESISTS CHANGE "And by the way, John Cornyn would have lost. It was just a point in time. John Cornyn would have lost by a lot. You know, one of those things. But he was beaten in the primary. And he's - he feels badly about it," the president continued. "He's a nice guy, John Cornyn, but he's doing a tremendous disservice because Gaiser is fantastic," Trump added. Cornyn wrote on X later Saturday, "If President Trump wanted to fill a judicial vacancy in Dallas, why did he wait until after the midterms to nominate someone? "The seat has been vacant since 2025. Then, without any consultation, he nominates a non-Texan with little connection to the Lone Star State, with no trial court experience, and who has not been appropriately vetted for a lifetime job. The Senate has a constitutional responsibility to provide 'advise and consent,' which is impossible without consultation," Cornyn added. "Still, I would like to work with the President to fill the seat while we still have a Senate majority. I have forwarded an outstanding candidate who was highly rated by Senator Cruz's and my bipartisan Federal Judicial Evaluation Committee, and who has now been interviewed by White House Counsel. All that is needed is an FBI background check with they stand ready to do on a timely basis," Cornyn also said. "Back to you, Mr. President. Time is of the essence." CORNYN MEETS WITH SEN-ELECT TALARICO, DESCRIBES HIM AS 'BASICALLY ... A GOOD PERSON' Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, called Cornyn's move "really frustrating," describing to Fox News' "Saturday in America" a tense encounter he had with Cornyn this week in Washington. "I came to him on the Senate floor, and I asked him to please let this judge go. And I tried to make the case on the merits that he'd make a fantastic judge. And I asked him, 'Will you just meet with him?' Because Cornyn refused even to meet with him," Cruz said. "He wouldn't talk to him. He just said, 'no, no, no.' And I was asking him, I said, 'Look, you're going to give this seat to the Democrats. Why would you want to do that?' And unfortunately, he got very angry. He began screaming. He began cursing at me," Cruz added. Cruz said, following the Republican losses in the midterm elections, "all the Republicans agreed, let's do everything humanly possible to confirm every judge we can before the end of the year, because we know the Democrats are going to come in January, and I expect they're going to block all judicial confirmations." TRUMP'S SUPREME COURT MAJORITY FACES LOOMING THREAT AFTER DEM SENATE TAKEOVER: 'STUCK' "We had two vacancies in Texas, one in Austin that we're moving forward with. And we'll have that judge confirmed by the end of the year. We had a second vacancy in Dallas, and the problem was that we did not have time to have a brand new nominee go through the paperwork, the FBI background check," Cruz told Fox News. "That takes weeks and weeks and weeks, and we simply didn't have time between now and the end of the year to get that done. And so the White House proposed a different idea, which is to go with a senior lawyer at the Department of Justice, a man named Eliot Gaiser, an incredibly qualified judicial nominee. "This is someone who was a law clerk at the U.S. Supreme Court for Justice Sam Alito. He was a state solicitor general arguing cases before the United States Supreme Court," Cruz said. "And he's right now the head of the Office of Legal Counsel, which is the senior constitutional advisor to the president and the senior constitutional advisor to the attorney general." Cruz also told Fox News he interviewed Gaiser and called him "incredibly principled, smart, capable, ready." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Cruz added, Gaiser "was a fantastic nomination. I was enthusiastic. Unfortunately, my colleague John Cornyn decided to block the nomination and any one senator can block a district court nomination from your state. "And so Cornyn did what's called — he refused to return the blue slip, which basically means he vetoed it — and the result of that is the seat is going to remain vacant. The people of Dallas are not going to have a judge in that seat. And he basically gave the seat to the Democrats," Cruz said. Fox News Digital's Alex Miller contributed to this report.

articles.title: The fight against fraud gets a makeover — we have seen this look before
articles.summary: As political power shifts in Washington, the debate continues between Democratic ‘pay and chase’ models and Republican ‘friction’ strategies regarding how the government will address systemic fraud and improper payments.
articles.body:
As political power shifts in Washington, expect a dramatic change in how government handles fraud. While candidates on both sides of the aisle frequently vow on the campaign trail to crack down on bad actors, their enforcement strategies differ widely. For instance, Minnesota Gov.-elect Amy Klobuchar (D) recently promised a “top-to-bottom audit” to fix a system in which millions of taxpayer dollars have gone missing. To the average voter, that sounds like tough action. But in fraud-prevention circles, a “post-payment audit” means “pay and chase,” sending government funds out the door first and trying to track down stolen cash after it’s already gone.

To understand the core debate, picture public assistance and benefit programs as a vast, open desert. The Republican approach is best described as the friction strategy. It litters the desert with “landmines” and imposes strict prepayment verification, identity checks and work requirements. The goal is upfront prevention — make it so difficult and risky to steal that fraudsters don’t bother crossing in the first place.

The Democratic approach prioritizes low friction, quick approvals, and minimal red tape so that eligible citizens receive help immediately. However, removing those administrative hurdles effectively clears the desert of landmines. Fraudsters move unchecked, and the government investigates only after the crossers have vanished with the money. The trade-off is clear: a low-friction environment maximizes access for people in need, but it also creates an easy target for bad actors. However, without automated, real-time verification before payments go out, post-payment enforcement yields abysmal returns.

Less than five years ago, the Government Accountability Organization estimated that COVID-19 relief fraud amounted to more than $200 billion stolen from pandemic relief programs such as the Paycheck Protection Program and Economic Injury Disaster Loans . Today, federal authorities have recovered only a tiny fraction of that, estimated at less than 2 percent.

“Recovered” does not include court-ordered repayments or monies not collected. Much of this money is never recovered, because it’s quickly laundered through shell companies and offshore accounts. More recently, at the state level, we have witnessed the risks of low-friction programs, including Minnesota’s Feeding Our Future scandal ( where $250 million intended for child nutrition programs was stolen ) and widespread California healthcare and hospice fraud schemes .

Even more disturbing, the GAO estimates that the federal government’s improper payment rate across all agencies consistently exceeds $200 billion annually, with some estimating double that loss, driven primarily by post-payment recovery models. Under traditional Democratic policy frameworks, improper payments are often viewed as an unavoidable byproduct of complex bureaucracy rather than systemic theft, shifting the focus onto predatory corporate vendors rather than systemic fraud prevention.

The Republican approach isn’t perfect either. While the friction-heavy model prevents more theft upfront it often devolves into performative crime-fighting and press conferences. Federal agencies regularly boast about announcing $100 million fraud busts. But a closer look shows the cases in question are often four to eight years old , and the recovery rate is frequently under 2 percent because the assets vanished long ago.

And even though the policy focus centers on hiring prosecutors to try cases, frontline field agents and boots-on-the-ground auditors have seen their ranks steadily decimated. Adding courtrooms doesn’t help if investigators can’t gather evidence in real time.

Most fraud experts agree that you cannot audit your way out of systemic fraud. If Washington truly wants to protect taxpayers while maintaining help for those who need it, Congress must move away from outdated “pay and chase” models and invest in real-time, automated pre-payment verification.

Without stopping fraudulent transactions before the check is mailed, expanding program spending will keep funding unrecoverable losses. That said, the incoming Congress’s focus on restoring federal funding to SNAP, bringing back ObamaCare subsidies, and a plethora of other free or subsidized programs may be welcome news to those wanting a redo. Make no mistake, domestic and transnational crime groups, and even the individual recipient, see the sign on the government halls being rewritten: “Free money, few questions asked.”

What remains to be seen is what actually happens next. Some state governors can no longer hide the systematic fraud uncovered in their benefit programs, and the media, both conservative and independent, and from time to time the mainstream media, will remind them they’re being watched. It’s not the current fight against fraud we should worry about during this transition but rather the future of fraud.

While the government says it’s modernizing its systems, rewriting its antiquated rules and regulations, and going after all fraud, the pool of money is now shrinking in favor of the recipient and, hence, the fraudster. Identity theft, deepfakes, phishing, and other high-tech fraud will all be unleashed on the taxpayer the second they realize the desert is free of mines and their time to cross is now, before the next change takes place. We must face the reality that fraud and complex fraud rings are not going anywhere. They’re more resilient and, like a factory, keep retooling, making way for more innovative ways to steal our money. Stay tuned.

Mark Haskins, Ph.D., is the former branch chief for the U.S. Department of Agriculture Special Investigations Unit, a retired law enforcement officer and a subject matter expert on government waste, fraud and abuse.

articles.title: Voters want to 'move on' from the president, former Trump official claims as reason for GOP's midterm defeat
articles.summary: Former Kansas Republican Sen. Sam Brownback says voters rejected President Trump himself, not his policies, citing inflation and gas prices.
articles.body: Former Kansas Republican Sen. Sam Brownback, who served as an ambassador during Donald Trump's first term, blamed the president's personal leadership style for Republicans' midterm losses. He claims the outcome of the 2026 elections — where Democrats' sweeping victories in traditional red strongholds helped them reclaim majorities in the House and Senate — was a sign of voters rejecting Trump more than rebuking his policies. "I think the thing we're missing is that it was really targeted at President Trump. I don't think it was targeted at the policies so much," Brownback told Fox News Digital in an interview. "Pride comes before a fall and a haughty spirit before a stumble." REPUBLICANS TURN ON TRUMP AFTER DEVASTATING MIDTERM LOSSES HAND DEMOCRATS CONTROL OF CONGRESS The former Kansas governor argued that Republicans should not write off the midterm results as the typical losses suffered by a president’s party through history during their second term. Brownback, who represented Kansas in the U.S. Senate from 1996 to 2011 before serving as governor from 2011 to 2018, said economic concerns, including inflation and gas prices, played a role in the election results. He suggested voters' frustrations extended beyond the economy to Trump's approach to governing. The Fox News Voter Poll found that 89% of voters considered the cost of living a crucial or major factor in their congressional vote, compared with 74% who said the same about the war in Iran. The findings suggest broader economic frustrations were also a major concern among voters, although the two issues may overlap and the polling does not establish which ultimately drove Republican defections. DEMS SEIZE ON MIDTERM ROUT TO DEMAND ICE REFORM, BUT POLLS REVEAL A TWIST IN WHO PRIORITIZED IMMIGRATION "People just saying I'm ready to move on past President Trump," Brownback said, adding that voters still appreciated the administration's efforts to secure the border but viewed interior immigration enforcement as too aggressive. The former ambassador-at-large for international religious freedom also urged Republicans to reconsider how they communicate with voters, emphasizing the importance of humility and kindness. "You just can't be proud. You've got to come forward humbly," Brownback said. "And I think you have to do that with the American public." Brownback called for a more measured response to voters' concerns ahead of 2028. "We hear you, American public. We're adjusting to the message that we heard," he said. REPUBLICANS NEED HISTORY LESSON ABOUT THEIR PARTY IF THEY WANT TO MOVE ON FROM DEFEAT "America is great because it's good. If it ever loses its goodness, it will lose its greatness," he added. "There has to be, as I keep doubling back to, a humility and a kindness about it as well." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Both Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio have been floated as potential contenders for the 2028 Republican presidential nomination, with Vance saying he plans to decide whether to launch a White House bid in the spring.

articles.title: Cruz says he is already working with Talarico on bringing Space Academy to Texas
articles.summary: Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) said he had a productive conversation with Sen.-elect James Talarico (D-Texas), his soon-to-be Texas partner, and that they will both push to bring President Trump’s proposed Space Academy to Texas. “I did actually spend a probably half hour on the phone with him yesterday talking about the space academy,” Cruz told…
articles.body:
Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) said he had a productive conversation with Sen.-elect James Talarico (D-Texas), his soon-to-be Texas partner, and that they will both push to bring President Trump’s proposed Space Academy to Texas.

“I did actually spend a probably half hour on the phone with him yesterday talking about the space academy,” Cruz told Fox News’s Kayleigh McEnany in an interview Saturday. “The president announced he’s going to create a Space Academy and James Talarico and I agreed to work together hand in hand … it belongs in Texas.”

Trump signed an executive order establishing the U.S. Space Academy in August, aimed at recruiting and training astronauts, engineers, scientists and more professionals for space exploration.

Cruz said he asked Talarico to join his push to open up the Space Academy in Houston, where NASA’s Johnson Space Center is located. Ohio and Florida, home to the Kennedy Space Center, are also making their pitch.

“I said to James, look I think it would be really powerful if we had a bipartisan commitment to fight for the Space Academy being in Texas … he was enthusiastic, he said he was eager to work with me on that, and so we’re gonna do it together.”

Talarico became the first Democrat to win statewide in more than 30 years when he pulled off a stunning victory in the Texas Senate race earlier this month, defeating Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton by more than 12 points.

Cruz called Talarico’s victory “impressive,” and recently offered to get coffee or tequila with the senator-elect to discuss how they could work together across party lines.

Since pulling off the win, Talarico has spoken with both of the Lone Star State’s GOP senators, meeting with Sen. John Cornyn while in Washington. Cornyn, who Talarico is replacing in the Senate, said he would be “cheering him on” if he did “a good job” representing Texas, and pledged to do all he could to help him during the transition.

The outgoing senator agreed that Talarico and Cruz would work together, saying he did not think they had a choice.

“They’re going to have to work together, represent 32 million people,” Cornyn told TMZ earlier this month. “I’m sure they’ll work it out, and because I’m sure they both have the best interest of the people of Texas at heart.”

articles.title: Trump on reported FBI hack: ‘I always like to put things in a positive spin’
articles.summary: President Trump said Saturday the potential breach of the FBI’s nationwide criminal information database is “not good,” but it may provide an opportunity to “learn things that we would have never learned otherwise.” “I always like to put things on a positive spin,” Trump said during a phone interview with Fox News’s “Saturday in America”…
articles.body:
President Trump said Saturday the potential breach of the FBI’s nationwide criminal information database is “not good,” but it may provide an opportunity to “learn things that we would have never learned otherwise.”

“I always like to put things on a positive spin,” Trump said during a phone interview with Fox News’s “Saturday in America ” when asked about the reports.

CNN reported Friday night the FBI’s National Crime Information Center — a nationwide database connecting federal, state and local law enforcement agencies — had been hacked. Trump did not confirm these reports in his Fox appearance, instead pivoting to discuss his unfounded voter fraud claims and “hoaxes” regarding Russia and Ukraine.

“You had the Russia, Russia, Russia hoax. You had all of these other hoaxes. We call it Ukraine, the Ukraine, Ukraine, Ukraine hoax … the perfect phone call, as I say,” Trump said, referring to his now infamous 2019 call in which he asked Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to investigate former President Biden — who was running for office at the time.

“You have so many other things. And maybe we’ll learn about them,” the president continued. “Maybe we’ll learn about the voter fraud, all the voter fraud that took place.”

Neither Trump nor the FBI have publicly verified the alleged data breach, and the agency did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment. But the reports came as the country grapples with an influx of widespread technology outages over the past week, impacting aviation, banking, email services and more.

It started with Microsoft’s global outages last week, impacting platforms like Outlook and Teams. A day later, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a rare nationwide ground stop that lasted more than four hours due to telecommunication issues, delaying or cancelling thousands of flights in the following days.

The following week, customers of several banks — including Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo — had trouble accessing their accounts.

Speculations flared over whether the outages were linked to a cyberattack, but Trump administration officials, including Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, have repeatedly asserted this not the case.

Amid the buzz, the Justice Department and the Department of Homeland Security announced a new hub on Wednesday seeking to combat cybercrime. The same week, Trump fired his national cyber director.

On Thursday, the White House tapped Kirsten Davies, the Pentagon’s chief information officer, to service as the acting cyber chief after Sean Cairncross’s removal.

articles.title: Trump praises 'reasonable guy' Hakeem Jeffries while touting 'ultimate' veto power over Democrats
articles.summary: President Donald Trump says bipartisanship with Hakeem Jeffries could deliver "tremendous things," touting healthcare and a 10% credit card rate cap.
articles.body: President Donald Trump reiterated his push for bipartisanship Saturday, saying he is confident he can work with Democratic congressional leaders to accomplish "tremendous things" when a divided government convenes in January. Speaking on "Saturday in America," Trump called House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., a "reasonable guy" and pointed to several issues they may be able to work on together. However, he warned that he is still prepared to use his veto power if Democrats refuse to negotiate. "There's a chance we could get great healthcare and a lot of other things, and we can do it in a bipartisan way," Trump told host Kayleigh McEnany. "There's a very good chance. Because otherwise, everything gets vetoed." TRUMP CONGRATULATES DEMOCRATS AFTER DOMINANT MIDTERMS, SAYS HE LOOKS FORWARD TO WORKING WITH THEM "I mean, I could sit there for two years and one month and just veto everything," he added. "Veto everything. And nothing would get done for anyone, and that's not the way to go." Jeffries ran unchallenged for House speaker on Wednesday, becoming speaker-designate in the internal caucus vote before a full House floor vote in January. In comments after the vote, Jeffries brushed off opposition from the progressive wing of his party and said he expects Democrats will be able to "work together." HAKEEM JEFFRIES WINS OVERWHELMING SPEAKER-DESIGNATE VOTE AS PROGRESSIVES' REVOLT FALLS FLAT Only 11 Democrats voted against Jeffries' nomination in the secret-ballot vote. Among those who opposed him — or publicly said they intended to — were Reps.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier, Adam Hamawy, Frederick D. Haynes III, Melat Kiros, Donavan McKinney, Chris Rabb and Claire Valdez. Trump said he looks "forward to working with Hakeem" and congratulated the Democrat on his win. "What he did was pretty spectacular with getting that position," Trump said. "And it's nice, the first Black person in that position, it's a big deal. It's a big deal, and he should be very proud of himself." Trump also pushed back on criticism from Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., over his recent trip to China, arguing that he feels the need to maintain relationships and an "open line of communication" with other world leaders. Still, Trump expressed optimism that he and congressional Democrats can work together, pointing to healthcare, the upcoming debt ceiling and a potential 10% cap on credit card interest rates as areas for compromise. "I think there's a — and I may be wrong. I may be wrong. But I think there's a real good chance they'll be sending stuff up, and rather than vetoing it — probably we'll start with vetoes just to set the stage," Trump said, adding that "the power of the veto is ultimate." TRUMP PLEDGES TO VETO 'INSANE' DEM BILLS, PINPOINTS ISSUE PARTIALLY TO BLAME FOR REPUBLICAN LOSSES "There's a chance that we can do better than we did when we had a very small majority with the Republicans," he continued. "They have some good points on healthcare, and they have some bad points. And we have some good things, and probably they would say we have some bad things. But there's a chance we could get great healthcare and a lot of other things, and we do it in a bipartisan way." articles.title: Trump praises Jeffries’s Speakership nod despite Stephen Miller jabs
articles.summary: President Trump offered up rare praise for House Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries (D) on Saturday morning, after the newly-nominated Democratic leader slammed his chief of staff Stephen Miller as a “stone-cold racist.” In an interview with Fox News’s Kayleigh McEnany on “Saturday in America,” Trump defended his top aide as a “good person.” “I think Hakeem…
articles.body:
President Trump offered up rare praise for House Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries (D) on Saturday morning, after the newly-nominated Democratic leader slammed his chief of staff Stephen Miller as a “stone-cold racist.”

In an interview with Fox News’s Kayleigh McEnany on “Saturday in America,” Trump defended his top aide as a “good person.”

“I think Hakeem will see that,” he said, adding that he “look[ed] forward” to working with the Democratic leader in the next Congress.

“I give him a lot of congratulations,” Trump continued. “What he did was pretty spectacular, with getting that position. And it’s nice: first Black person in that position — it’s a big deal. It’s a big deal, and he should be very proud of himself.”

In an interview with The New York Times published Saturday, Jeffries said he could not imagine sitting down to negotiate with the White House chief of staff.

“No. I made clear that Stephen Miller’s a stone-cold racist,” he told the Times’s Lulu Garcia-Navarro.

“Why would I deal with him at this point in time?” he continued. “This is the architect of Donald Trump’s violent mass deportation machine, and there’s cruelty associated with that. There’s chaos. There’s death associated with what’s taking place.”

Jeffries also told the Times that House Minority Leader-designate Jim Jordan (R) has contacted him, but Trump and Vice President JD Vance have not following his nomination to lead his party in the House.

While Trump indicated his openness to working with Jeffries and other Democrats on bipartisan legislation, he emphasized his veto power, saying, “Look, I have the power.”

“There’s a chance we could get great healthcare and a lot of other things, and we do it in a bipartisan way,” he told McEnany. “There’s a very good chance because otherwise everything gets vetoed.

“I could sit there for two years and one month and just veto everything,” he continued. “Veto everything, and nothing would get done for anyone and that’s not the way to go.”

Trump also expressed optimism about working with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), who is facing a challenge for majority leader from Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.).

“I know Chuck Schumer well, and I think what happens is we have a chance to do something historic,” he said. “They’re going to their points across, I’ll get our points across — meaning a more conservative view — and there’s a chance we could do tremendous things on healthcare and maybe even we can touch the subject of immigration.”

articles.title: Washington governor decries ‘out-of-control’ ICE at Seattle airport
articles.summary: Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson (D) condemned Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) operations at the Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday, in which masked federal agents detained two people. The Democratic governor responded to a report from The Seattle Times on the incident, calling ICE “completely and totally out of control.” “ICE is completely and totally out…
articles.body:
Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson (D) condemned Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) operations at the Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday, in which masked federal agents detained two people.

The Democratic governor responded to a report from The Seattle Times on the incident, calling ICE “completely and totally out of control.”

“ICE is completely and totally out of control,” Ferguson wrote in a social media post . “Like many Americans, I’m outraged by masked agents, who do not identify themselves, dragging people off jetways as they board a flight, creating chaos in our communities.

“Today’s actions at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport are just the latest example of ICE’s deeply un-American tactics,” he continued.

Ferguson reshared a video that depicted masked federal officers dragging a person away while a woman screamed that her daughter was being taken away and said, “We have a work permit.”

At an afternoon press conference, the governor called this video “horrific” and “chilling.”

“We need a system of immigration enforcement and border security that is effective, ethical and humane, and ICE is not it,” Ferguson said. “It is beyond reform.”

In a statement to the Associated Press , ICE said its officers conducted a targeted operation to detain Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, a Mexican immigrant who “overstayed his visa in violation of our nation’s laws.”

ICE told AP that a woman — Sofia Hernandez Mejia — “hurled hot coffee on the officers” and was determined to also be in the U.S. illegally from Mexico and overstayed her visa. She could face charges for assaulting a federal officer, according to the law enforcement agency.

The Port of Seattle, which operates the airport, said in a statement that it was “outraged” by the incident and that federal officers acted “without the Port’s participation or knowledge.”

“This incident was not only distressing for the affected family but the passengers around them, and Port officials continue to engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred,” the statement read .

Washington Rep. Adam Smith (D) also condemned the arrest as “absolutely unacceptable” in a statement shared by his office on Saturday.

“I am incredibly concerned about the conduct of immigration enforcement and believe that ICE is operating as a paramilitary force that is a profound threat to our community,” he wrote. “There is no question that this agency needs to be reined in before causing more chaos and fear.”

In August, a 23-year-old asylum seeker was detained at the Seattle airport after she returned from vacation. The woman was detained by federal officers when she deboarded the plane to get on a connecting flight to Houston.

The Hill has reached out to ICE for comment.
